title: The elephant in the pool
hookLine: plunge into good work like an elephant into a cool pool in the heat (Bodhicaryavatara 7)
tomorrow: once you're in, what keeps you going?

cards: The task has been sitting there for days: the email to a teacher, the hard conversation, the form with too many boxes. Every time you look at it, you dip a toe in and pull back.

The water feels cold, and so does the dread. And yet, when you finally jump, the shock lasts about a second. Shantideva has a picture for what to do next, and it comes from watching elephants on a hot afternoon.

teach.h: AN ELEPHANT IN THE MIDDAY HEAT.
teach.b: An elephant, tormented by the midday heat, comes to a pool. It doesn't test the water. It doesn't circle the edge.
It plunges in, the whole huge body, and the relief is immediate. That, says Shantideva, is how to enter the good task in front of you.
Not with dread, as if the water were cold, but like the overheated elephant, because the work itself is the relief.

Just before it, he adds a line about appetite: people never seem to get enough of pleasures, so why get enough of good work? It flips how we usually see it. We treat the hard task as the heat and avoiding it as the shade.
Shantideva says it's the other way around.
The circling is the heat: checking, rereading, waiting to feel ready.

The task is the pool. In an ordinary week that might mean opening the document and typing the first rough sentence before the mind files its objections. Or saying the hard thing in the first minute of the call.
This is virya at work. You don't have to love the water first. You find out it's cool once you're in.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes use Shantideva's elephant image to encourage beginning practice or service wholeheartedly, without waiting for the right mood.

games.q: what does “the elephant in the pool” mean?
o: a huge problem that everyone sees but no one names
relaxing in cool water after finishing a hard job
entering good work wholeheartedly, without hesitating

games.q: the elephant's lesson — tap the pairs.

s: in Shantideva's picture, the elephant tests the water before going in
it plunges straight in, the whole body, and the relief is immediate.
Shantideva compares the good task to the cool water, not to the heat
the circling and the dread are the heat; the work is the relief.

games.q: your brother has put off calling the landlord about the broken heater for a week. which advice fits the elephant?
o: call now, and say the problem in the very first sentence.
write out a perfect script first, then call once he feels calm.
wait for the weekend, when there's more time to handle it.
games.why: the elephant doesn't circle the edge. the waiting is the heat; the call is the pool.

practice: Name the task you've been circling, and on any scrap of paper, write its very first line by hand: the greeting of the email, the opening sentence, the first box on the form. Don't fix it.
Then rest your hand on what you wrote, and breathe like someone already in the water.

wordCard.voice: The elephant in the pool: Shantideva's picture of entering good work whole, like a hot elephant plunging into cool water.

carryVoice: Keep this close: into the pool, because the circling was the hot part. Four days of chapter seven, done.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 7.64-7.65 (insatiable for good deeds; like an elephant scorched by the midday sun plunging into a pool)
